extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, and judges (and advanced law students) dealing with re-issue patent applications and litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and doctrines for determining whether a re-issued patent is for the same invention as the original, what amendments are permissible, and how to construe re-issues (including special rules for machine patents, use of models/drawings, evidentiary limits, and the role of inadvertence vs. fraud).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of identity between re-issue and original
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention claimed in a re-issue is presumed to be identical with that attempted to be patented in the original until the contrary appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption is strong and rebuttable only by strong and controlling evidence (usually a comparison of the two specifications and related papers). Cases cited (e.g., Spaeth v. Barney) treat the Commissioner's allowance as prima facie evidence that re-issue is lawful, and the presumption in favor of validity and identity is substantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity determined by comparing instruments as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity of the re-issue with the original is ascertained by comparing the drawings, specifications, and model as a whole rather than piecemeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proper inquiry is a comparison of the two patents (and drawings/models) in view of their terms and import; if, when so construed, the inventions are not substantially different the re-issue must be held valid. Courts will adopt interpretations to uphold rather than destroy rights where reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stricter test for machine patents: drawings/models control
rubrics_metrics.description: For a machine-patent the identity of the re-issue with the original is determined by a stricter, more conclusive test: compare models and drawings, and nothing can be embraced in the re-issue that is not found in the models or drawings annexed to the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A machine can be exactly represented pictorially or by model; failure to indicate essential parts in the drawings/model suggests the inventor did not comprehend the invention. This rule prevents imperceptible structural changes from producing a new machine by re-issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: When invention cannot be represented pictorially, extrinsic evidence allowed with limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions incapable of representation by drawings or models may be interpreted by extrinsic (parol) evidence, but such proof must be satisfactory to the Commissioner and not inconsistent with the original specification, drawings, and model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute permits proof 'satisfactory to the Commissioner' to show omitted matter was part of the original invention; however, admitting parol evidence alone to introduce a substantially different invention is forbidden as it invites fraud. Original Patent Office papers and official actions are commonly considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection of original drawings and models permissible and often decisive
rubrics_metrics.description: The original drawings and model filed may be examined to determine the identity of the re-issue with the original; a feature absent from the specification/drawings may be found in the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a feature is claimed in the re-issue but not in the drawings/specification, inspection of the original model can determine whether the feature was present; where model is not produced it may be presumed to contain the feature unless rebutted. Dilapidated models may be aided by evidence of their primitive condition if consistent with drawings/description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost model — strict standard to alter drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the model is lost and the drawings are said to be incorrect, no change can be permitted in the drawings to cure the defect except upon the most conclusive evidence that the invention, as presented in the model, would have justified the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require the clearest proof before permitting alteration of drawings in absence of the original model (Royer v. Russell and similar authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: No addition of new matter that changes character of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot introduce matter that changes the character of the invention originally patented; new claims that change the nature of the invention are not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The re-issue statute is intended to correct inadvertence, accident, or mistake in the original; it is not a vehicle to claim a substantially different invention. Authorities (e.g., Flower v. Detroit) find insufficient basis for new claims that alter the original invention's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue construed in light of the original and the state of the art at original date
rubrics_metrics.description: Description, drawings, and model of the re-issue are to be construed, if possible, so as to confine the re-issue to the original invention and in view of the state of the art at the time the original patent was granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state of the art when the original was filed may be shown to interpret identity. Courts attempt to construe re-issues so as to cover the real invention claimed in the original; liberal construction is applied to preserve rights if reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's allowance is prima facie evidence and final absent clear excess
rubrics_metrics.description: The allowance by the Commissioner of a surrender and re-issue is prima facie evidence of lawful re-issue and is final and conclusive unless it is apparent on the face of the patent that he exceeded his authority or there is repugnancy between old and new patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent suits will not re-examine the Commissioner's decision unless the court can, from the patent itself, see that the Commissioner exceeded statutory authority; long lists of cases illustrate limited judicial re-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims of re-issue confined to original invention where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of a re-issued patent should be construed, if possible, to cover only the real invention described in the original; claims apparently in excess should be limited by construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Void claims in a re-issue do not impair the validity of original claims repeated in the re-issue; courts may strike or construe void parts while preserving valid portions. A patentee may disclaim void matter in the Patent Office to preserve valid claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue allowed only for inadvertence, accident, or mistake (no fraud)
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment by re-issue is permitted only when the imperfections in the original patent arose from inadvertence, accident, or mistake and without any fraudulent or deceptive intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fraud or wilful deception renders the patent void ab initio and unamendable by re-issue. Applicant must show the defect arose innocently; diligence and good faith are required. The doctrine rests on statute and public-policy grounds that omitted matter voluntarily or knowingly omitted is abandoned to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Inadvertence' refers to the application not the invention; error of judgment not enough
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Inadvertence, etc.' exists in reference to the application (i.e., omission in filing/claiming), not to the invention; an error in opinion or judgment is not a 'mistake or inadvertence' sufficient for re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants cannot use re-issue to insert claims omitted because they thought them unpatentable. Ex parte Mahnken and related authorities establish the limits; re-issue creates immediate evidence of inadvertence but can be rebutted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original Patent Office papers and re-issue file may be consulted
rubrics_metrics.description: Original papers filed in the Patent Office and the files of the re-issue application may be examined to show scope and identity of the re-issue with the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commissioner may consider all original papers, prior official actions, and other evidence to determine whether omitted matter was part of the original invention; files of the re-issue application can be resorted to for resolving doubts about scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption favoring validity of re-issue; heavy burden to show otherwise
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a strong general presumption in favor of the validity of a re-issue and the identity of the inventions; rebutting this presumption requires strong and controlling evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous cases emphasize the weight of this presumption; a re-issue granted after contest or delay will still be presumed valid unless clear proof of excess or departure exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay in seeking re-issue affects construction (long delay disfavors broadening)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a re-issue broadening the claims is granted after a significant delay (e.g., four and a half years), courts will construe it as covering the same matter as the original rather than allowing broadened scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long delay may be evidence that the patentee sought to enlarge rights; courts are reluctant to allow materially broader scope after long intervening periods (see Albany Steam Trap Co. v. Felthonsen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Void claims in re-issue do not necessarily invalidate other claims; disclaimers allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Void claims in a re-issue can be rejected or disclaimed without prejudice to properly allowed claims, and void claims do not necessarily affect the validity of other claims in the same re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will often reject void portions while preserving valid claims; patentees may record disclaimers in the Patent Office to remove improperly claimed matter and maintain suits on the remaining valid claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question of identity is one of construction, not merely evidence, when patents are understandable
rubrics_metrics.description: When a court can understand the inventions from the patents themselves, the question of identity between a re-issue and its original is one of construction rather than of evidentiary proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patents (and drawings/models) themselves enable comparison, courts will resolve identity by construing the instruments rather than admitting extensive extrinsic proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model evidence may be established by other testimony if lost or destroyed
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a model is lost or destroyed it may nevertheless be established by parol or other evidence to support the re-issue (subject to limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as Meyer v. Goodyear's India Rubber Glove Mfg. Co. show that lost models can sometimes be proved by other evidence, but such proof must not conflict with original specifications and is scrutinized closely.
